description: Run a pre-mortem using the Gary Klein method: imagine the project has already failed, work backward to identify the most likely causes, then address them before they happen. Prevention is cheaper than recovery.

steps.description: Capture the current project plan, assumptions, timeline, and success criteria as the baseline for the pre-mortem.

inputs.name: project-plan
inputs.desc: The current project plan with milestones and timeline

inputs.name: success-criteria
inputs.desc: What success looks like in specific, measurable terms

outputs.name: plan-snapshot
outputs.desc: The project plan frozen at this moment, including all stated assumptions

outputs.name: assumption-list
outputs.desc: Every assumption the plan depends on, extracted and listed explicitly

process: Write down the plan as it exists today: milestones, dates, dependencies, owners, and the definition of success.

Extract every assumption embedded in the plan. A plan that says 'launch by March' assumes the team is available, the technology works, approvals come through, and no competitor moves first. Make each assumption explicit.
For each assumption, rate how confident you are that it will hold (high, medium, low). Low-confidence assumptions are the first candidates for failure causes.
Identify any dependencies on external parties or events you do not control. These are the highest-risk elements because you cannot fix them by working harder.

steps.description: Gather the team and announce: 'It is 6 months from now. The project has failed completely. Write down why it failed.'

outputs.name: failure-stories
outputs.desc: Each participant's independent story of how and why the project failed

outputs.name: raw-failure-causes
outputs.desc: All failure causes mentioned across all stories, with duplicates preserved to show frequency

process: Announce the frame: 'Imagine we are 6 months in the future. This project has failed badly. It is not a small miss; it is a complete failure. I want each of you to write down, independently, the story of how it failed. What went wrong? Why?'
Give each person 10 minutes to write in silence. No discussion. Independent writing prevents groupthink and ensures quiet team members contribute their concerns.
Go around the room and have each person read one failure cause. Continue rounds until all causes are stated. Do not allow debate or pushback during this phase. The goal is collection, not evaluation.

Record every cause mentioned. Preserve duplicates: if three people independently say 'the vendor missed the deadline,' that convergence is a stronger signal than a unique cause mentioned by one person.

steps.description: Cluster the raw failure causes into themes and rank them by likelihood and impact.

inputs.name: raw-failure-causes
inputs.desc: All failure causes from the imagination session

inputs.name: assumption-list
inputs.desc: The assumptions from the plan snapshot

outputs.name: failure-themes
outputs.desc: Failure causes grouped by theme (e.g., team capacity, technical risk, market shift, dependency failure)

outputs.name: ranked-risks
outputs.desc: Each theme ranked by: likelihood (how many people mentioned it) times impact (how badly it would hurt)

process: Group the raw causes into 5-8 themes. Similar causes cluster together: 'developer quit' and 'team burned out' are both team capacity risks.
Count the frequency of each theme. A theme mentioned by 4 of 6 participants is more likely than one mentioned by 1.
Rate each theme on impact: if this failure cause materialized, how badly would it damage the project? Use a 1-10 scale.
Rank themes by likelihood times impact. The top 3 are the pre-mortem's priority findings. These are the failure modes the team collectively believes are both probable and dangerous.

steps.description: For each top-ranked failure theme, design a specific prevention action that can be taken now.

inputs.name: ranked-risks
inputs.desc: Failure themes ranked by likelihood times impact

outputs.name: prevention-actions
outputs.desc: For each top 3 failure theme: one specific action to take now that reduces either the likelihood or the impact

outputs.name: plan-modifications
outputs.desc: Changes to the project plan that incorporate the prevention actions

process: For each top failure theme, ask: can we reduce the likelihood (prevent it from happening) or reduce the impact (limit the damage if it does happen)?

Design one specific, actionable prevention step for each. 'Monitor the vendor more closely' is too vague. 'Schedule weekly deliverable checkpoints with the vendor, with a contractual penalty clause for misses' is specific.
Integrate the prevention actions into the project plan as real tasks with owners and deadlines. A prevention action that is not in the plan will not happen.
Identify early warning indicators for each risk theme. What would you see in the first 2 weeks that signals this failure mode is developing? These become your monitoring triggers.

steps.description: Set up monitoring for the early warning indicators so the team can catch failure modes as they develop, not after they have materialized.

inputs.name: prevention-actions
inputs.desc: The prevention actions with early warning indicators

outputs.name: monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: Which indicators to watch, how often to check, who checks, and what action to take if the indicator triggers

outputs.name: escalation-protocol
outputs.desc: What happens when an early warning triggers: who gets told, what decision gets made, and how fast

process: For each early warning indicator, define: what to measure, how often to measure it, who is responsible for measuring it, and the threshold that triggers action.
Keep the monitoring lightweight. If checking an indicator takes more than 5 minutes per week, it will be skipped. Automate where possible.
Define the escalation path: when an indicator triggers, who needs to know within 24 hours, and what decision authority do they have? A warning that triggers no action is theater.

Schedule a pre-mortem review at the project midpoint to reassess: which risks materialized (and were caught), which did not, and whether new risks have emerged that the original session did not anticipate.

description: Apply the Theory of Constraints: find the ONE bottleneck in any system, improve only that bottleneck, then find the new bottleneck. Improving anything other than the bottleneck is waste because the system throughput is limited by its constraint.

steps.description: Map the system as a sequence of steps and measure the throughput capacity of each step independently.

inputs.name: system-description
inputs.desc: The system to audit (a business process, a production line, a personal workflow, a sales funnel, a software pipeline)

inputs.name: throughput-goal
inputs.desc: The desired throughput of the system (units per time period)

outputs.name: step-sequence
outputs.desc: The system mapped as a sequence of steps, each with its throughput capacity (units it can process per time period)

outputs.name: current-throughput
outputs.desc: The actual throughput of the whole system, which equals the throughput of the slowest step

process: Map the system as a linear sequence of steps from input to output. Even complex systems can usually be linearized for bottleneck analysis by following the main flow.
For each step, measure its independent capacity: how many units could this step process per time period if it had unlimited input and no downstream backup?

Identify the current throughput of the entire system. By definition, it equals the capacity of the slowest step. If step 3 can only process 50 units/day and every other step can process 100+, the system produces 50.
Verify by checking: is there inventory (work, tasks, leads, items) building up before any step? The step with the longest queue in front of it is likely the bottleneck.

steps.description: Identify the single bottleneck: the step with the lowest throughput capacity that limits the entire system.

inputs.name: step-sequence
inputs.desc: All steps with their throughput capacities

outputs.name: bottleneck-step
outputs.desc: The specific step that is the constraint, with its capacity and the evidence

outputs.name: bottleneck-cost
outputs.desc: The cost of the bottleneck: the difference between the bottleneck's capacity and the desired throughput, multiplied by the value of each unit

process: The bottleneck is the step with the lowest throughput capacity. In a factory, it is the slowest machine. In a sales funnel, it is the stage with the lowest conversion rate. In a personal workflow, it is the task you can never keep up with.
Confirm the bottleneck by checking three signs: (1) it is always busy, (2) the steps before it have queued work waiting, (3) the steps after it are sometimes idle.

Calculate the cost of the bottleneck: every unit the bottleneck cannot process is a unit the system cannot produce. Multiply the gap (desired throughput minus bottleneck capacity) by the value per unit.

Resist the temptation to identify multiple bottlenecks. There is only one. If you think there are two, the real bottleneck is the one that, if removed, would cause the other to become the new constraint.

steps.description: Before investing in expanding the bottleneck, exploit it: make sure you are getting 100% of its current capacity.

outputs.name: exploitation-actions
outputs.desc: Actions that increase the bottleneck's effective capacity without spending money: eliminate downtime, reduce defects that waste capacity, ensure the bottleneck never waits for input

outputs.name: capacity-after-exploitation
outputs.desc: The bottleneck's capacity after exploitation improvements

process: Audit how the bottleneck currently spends its time. Is it ever idle? Is it ever processing defective input that will be rejected later? Is it ever doing work that could be done by a non-bottleneck step?
Eliminate idle time at the bottleneck. It should never wait for input. Buffer work in front of it so it always has something to process.
Eliminate waste at the bottleneck. If 10% of the input is defective, quality-check BEFORE the bottleneck, not after. The bottleneck's time is too valuable to waste on bad input.
Move any work that does not strictly require the bottleneck to a non-bottleneck step. If the bottleneck is a specialist, have non-specialists handle prep and cleanup.

steps.description: Subordinate all other steps to the bottleneck: pace the entire system to the bottleneck's rhythm.

inputs.name: exploitation-actions
inputs.desc: How the bottleneck is being maximized

outputs.name: subordination-plan
outputs.desc: How each non-bottleneck step will be paced to the bottleneck's throughput (producing only as much as the bottleneck can consume)

outputs.name: waste-reduction
outputs.desc: Inventory and work-in-progress that will be reduced by subordinating

process: Set the pace of every step before the bottleneck to match the bottleneck's consumption rate. If the bottleneck processes 50 units/day, step 1 should produce 50 units/day, not 100. Overproduction before the bottleneck creates inventory that costs money and space.
Set the pace of every step after the bottleneck to process whatever the bottleneck outputs without delay. The bottleneck's output should never wait.
This feels counterintuitive: you are deliberately slowing down non-bottleneck steps. But a non-bottleneck step running at full speed creates waste (inventory) without increasing system throughput.
Measure work-in-progress inventory before and after subordination. A well-subordinated system has small, consistent buffers, not large, growing piles.

steps.description: If exploitation and subordination are not enough, invest in elevating the bottleneck: add capacity through spending.

inputs.name: capacity-after-exploitation
inputs.desc: The bottleneck capacity after free improvements

inputs.name: bottleneck-cost
inputs.desc: The cost of the remaining constraint

outputs.name: elevation-options
outputs.desc: Options for adding capacity to the bottleneck: hiring, equipment, automation, outsourcing, process redesign

outputs.name: elevation-roi
outputs.desc: For each option: cost to implement vs. value of the additional throughput it produces

process: List every option for adding capacity to the bottleneck. Common options: add a second instance (hire another person, buy another machine), automate part of the work, outsource part of the work, redesign the step to be faster.

For each option, calculate the ROI: the cost of the investment divided by the value of the additional throughput it produces. Because the bottleneck limits the entire system, even expensive investments at the bottleneck can have high ROI.
Implement the option with the highest ROI. Do not implement multiple options simultaneously; add capacity incrementally and measure the impact.
After elevating, re-measure the system. The former bottleneck may no longer be the constraint. A new step is now the bottleneck. Return to step 1 and repeat the cycle.

steps.description: After improving the bottleneck, detect where the new bottleneck has formed and restart the cycle.

outputs.name: new-system-throughput
outputs.desc: The system's throughput after the improvement

outputs.name: new-bottleneck
outputs.desc: The new constraint step, or confirmation that the system now meets the throughput goal

process: Re-measure the throughput capacity of every step, including the improved bottleneck.
The new bottleneck is the step that now has the lowest capacity. It may be the step that was second-slowest before, or it may be a step that was not previously close to being a constraint.
If the system now meets the throughput goal, stop. Do not optimize further. Over-optimization past the goal is waste.
If the system does not yet meet the goal, repeat the cycle: exploit the new bottleneck, subordinate other steps, and elevate if necessary. This is a continuous improvement loop, not a one-time event.

description: Solve problems by inversion: instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you would guarantee failure, then avoid those things. Produces better results than direct optimization because failure modes are more concrete than success paths.

steps.description: State the problem you are trying to solve in positive terms, then invert it.

inputs.name: problem-description
inputs.desc: The problem or goal stated normally (e.g., 'How do we increase customer retention?')

inputs.name: context
inputs.desc: The situation and constraints around the problem

outputs.name: positive-statement
outputs.desc: The goal stated positively: 'We want to achieve X'

outputs.name: inverted-statement
outputs.desc: The goal inverted: 'How would we guarantee the opposite of X? How would we make sure we LOSE customers?'

process: Write the goal in one sentence, positively: 'We want to [achieve something specific].'
Invert it: 'How would we guarantee the opposite? How would we make absolutely certain that we fail at this?'

The inversion should feel slightly absurd. 'How would we guarantee that every customer leaves?' That absurdity makes it easier to think of answers because failure modes are more vivid than success factors.
Write the inverted question on a whiteboard or at the top of a document. This is now the question everyone will answer.

steps.description: Brainstorm every way you could guarantee failure. Be specific and creative.

inputs.name: inverted-statement
inputs.desc: The inverted question: how to guarantee failure

outputs.name: failure-methods
outputs.desc: A complete list of specific actions that would guarantee failure (15-25 items)

outputs.name: categorized-failures
outputs.desc: The failure methods grouped by category (process failures, people failures, resource failures, timing failures, communication failures)

process: Generate at least 15 specific ways to guarantee failure. Examples for 'How to guarantee customers leave': ignore their support tickets, change the price without warning, break features they depend on, make the product harder to use with each update, never respond to feedback.
Be specific, not vague. 'Provide bad service' is too vague. 'Take 5 days to respond to support tickets and then send a generic non-answer' is specific.

Include the subtle failures, not just the obvious ones. Obvious: 'delete their data.' Subtle: 'make the cancellation process so easy that any frustrated moment leads to churn.' The subtle ones are more useful because they might already be happening.
Group the failures by category to see patterns. If most failure methods are communication failures, that tells you where the real risk is.

steps.description: Compare the failure list against your current behavior. Any overlap means you are already partially guaranteeing failure.

inputs.name: failure-methods
inputs.desc: All the ways to guarantee failure

outputs.name: overlap-list
outputs.desc: Failure methods that partially describe current behavior (things you are already doing that would guarantee failure)

outputs.name: severity-ranking
outputs.desc: The overlaps ranked by how closely your current behavior matches the failure method

process: Take each failure method and honestly ask: are we doing any version of this right now? Most teams will find 3-5 items on the failure list that they are partially doing.
Rate the severity of each overlap: 'fully doing this' (high severity), 'sometimes doing this' (medium), 'slightly doing this' (low).
The high-severity overlaps are emergencies. You are actively driving toward the failure you want to avoid.

This is the core value of inversion: it reveals problems you are blind to when thinking positively. 'How do we retain customers?' might produce generic answers. 'We are currently responding to support tickets in 4 days, which is one of our guaranteed failure methods' is specific and actionable.

steps.description: For each overlap, design the opposite action: the specific behavior change that moves away from failure.

inputs.name: overlap-list
inputs.desc: Things you are doing that partially guarantee failure

outputs.name: anti-failure-actions
outputs.desc: For each overlap: the specific opposite behavior to adopt, who owns it, and the deadline

outputs.name: success-indicators
outputs.desc: How to measure whether each anti-failure action is working

process: For each overlap, define the exact opposite behavior. If the failure method is 'respond to support tickets in 4+ days,' the anti-failure action is 'respond to every ticket within 4 hours.'
Make each action specific and owned. 'Improve support response time' is not an action. 'Hire one additional support agent by March 1 to bring average response time below 4 hours' is an action.
Prioritize by severity: fix the high-severity overlaps first. These are the items where you are most actively driving toward failure.
Define a success indicator for each action. The indicator should show whether you are moving away from the failure mode, not just whether you implemented the action.

steps.description: After implementing the anti-failure actions, re-run the inversion to check for new failure modes.

outputs.name: remaining-overlaps
outputs.desc: Any failure methods still partially in effect after the changes

outputs.name: new-failure-modes
outputs.desc: New failure methods that emerged as a result of the changes (fixing one problem sometimes creates another)

process: Re-run the failure guarantee brainstorm with the current state of the system. Some original failure methods should no longer overlap.
Check for new failure modes created by the changes. Sometimes fixing a support speed problem creates a support quality problem (rushing leads to shallow answers).
If new overlaps exist, repeat the cycle: design anti-failure actions for the new overlaps.
Schedule an inversion review quarterly. The failure landscape changes as the business changes, so the inversion needs to be refreshed.

description: Run a Pareto audit on any system: find the 20% of inputs producing 80% of outputs, then reallocate resources from the unproductive 80% to the productive 20%. Works for revenue, time, relationships, features, and customers.

steps.description: Collect the data on inputs and outputs: what are you putting in, and what results are you getting?

inputs.name: system-to-audit
inputs.desc: What you are auditing (revenue by customer, time by activity, features by usage, marketing channels by conversion)

inputs.name: time-period
inputs.desc: The period to analyze (last quarter, last year, last month)

outputs.name: input-output-data
outputs.desc: A table of inputs and their corresponding outputs, sorted by output volume descending

outputs.name: total-output
outputs.desc: The total output across all inputs

process: Define the input and output clearly. For revenue: input = customer, output = revenue. For time: input = activity, output = value produced. For features: input = feature, output = user sessions involving that feature.
Collect the data for the specified period. Use actual numbers, not estimates. Estimates are biased toward the inputs you pay attention to.
Sort the data by output descending: highest-output inputs first.
Calculate the total output. This is the denominator for calculating percentages.

steps.description: Analyze the distribution: what percentage of inputs produces what percentage of outputs? Plot the cumulative curve.

inputs.name: input-output-data
inputs.desc: Sorted table of inputs and outputs

outputs.name: pareto-curve
outputs.desc: Cumulative percentage: for each input added in order, what cumulative percentage of total output has been reached

outputs.name: pareto-ratio
outputs.desc: The actual ratio (e.g., 18% of customers produce 82% of revenue). It is rarely exactly 80/20 but the concentration is always present.

process: Calculate each input's share of total output as a percentage.
Build the cumulative curve: first input contributes X%, first two inputs contribute X+Y%, and so on.
Find the knee of the curve: the point where adding the next input contributes significantly less than the previous one. This separates the vital few from the trivial many.
State the actual Pareto ratio. It might be 15/85 or 25/75. The exact ratio does not matter; what matters is that a small number of inputs produce a disproportionate share of outputs.

steps.description: Deep-dive into the vital few (the top 20%): understand what makes them different and how to get more of them.

outputs.name: vital-few-profile
outputs.desc: The common characteristics of the top 20% of inputs (what do the best customers, highest-value activities, or most-used features have in common?)

outputs.name: replication-strategy
outputs.desc: How to find or create more inputs that match the vital-few profile

process: List the vital few (top 20% of inputs by output). What do they have in common? For customers: industry, size, use case, acquisition channel. For activities: type of work, time of day, who is involved.

The common characteristics of the vital few are your targeting criteria. If your best customers are all mid-market SaaS companies acquired through referrals, your growth strategy is: more mid-market SaaS referrals.
Identify what you are doing for the vital few that you are not doing for the rest. Sometimes the vital few produce more because they receive better service, not because they are inherently better.
Design a replication strategy: how to find or create more inputs that match the vital-few profile. This is your growth playbook.

steps.description: Triage the trivial many (the bottom 80%): decide which to cut, which to maintain, and which to try to upgrade.

outputs.name: cut-list
outputs.desc: Inputs in the bottom 80% that should be dropped because they consume resources and produce negligible output

outputs.name: maintain-list
outputs.desc: Inputs that produce modest output but require minimal resources

outputs.name: upgrade-candidates
outputs.desc: Inputs that resemble the vital few profile and might respond to more investment

process: For each input in the bottom 80%, calculate its cost-to-serve: how much time, money, or attention does it consume relative to its output?

Inputs with high cost-to-serve and low output are candidates for cutting. These are the customers who demand the most support but generate the least revenue, or the activities that take all day but produce nothing.
Inputs with low cost-to-serve and low output can be maintained on autopilot. They do not help much, but they do not cost much either.

Inputs that share characteristics with the vital-few profile but have not yet produced high output are upgrade candidates. They might respond to the same treatment that makes the vital few productive.

steps.description: Reallocate the resources freed from cutting the trivial many into expanding the vital few.

inputs.name: replication-strategy
inputs.desc: How to get more vital-few inputs

outputs.name: reallocation-plan
outputs.desc: Where each freed resource goes: to replication (finding more top performers), to upgrading (investing in promising inputs), or to deepening (serving existing top performers even better)

outputs.name: expected-impact
outputs.desc: The projected increase in total output from the reallocation

process: Calculate the resources freed by cutting the trivial many: hours of time, dollars of budget, attention capacity.

Allocate the freed resources to three buckets: replication (finding more vital-few-profile inputs), upgrading (investing in the upgrade candidates), and deepening (providing even better service to existing vital few to increase their output).

Estimate the expected impact. If the vital few produce 80% of output with 20% of resources, adding 50% more resources to them could produce significantly more output. The exact estimate depends on whether the vital few are capacity-constrained.
Implement the reallocation over 30-60 days and measure the impact. Re-run the Pareto audit at the end of the period to see whether the distribution has shifted.

description: Find the upstream intervention point where a small change prevents a large downstream problem. Most firefighting happens because nobody fixed the upstream cause. Map the causal chain from symptom to root, then intervene at the highest leverage point.

steps.description: List every symptom (downstream problem) you are currently fighting, without trying to fix any of them yet.

inputs.name: current-problems
inputs.desc: The recurring problems, complaints, failures, or firefighting that consumes your time

inputs.name: frequency-data
inputs.desc: How often each problem occurs (daily, weekly, monthly)

outputs.name: symptom-list
outputs.desc: Every recurring problem listed with its frequency, time cost per occurrence, and who handles it

outputs.name: total-firefighting-cost
outputs.desc: The total time and money spent fighting these symptoms per month

process: List every recurring problem you deal with. Include customer complaints, system outages, quality defects, team conflicts, missed deadlines, budget overruns.
For each symptom, record: how often it occurs, how long it takes to fix each time, who fixes it, and what the downstream impact is if it is not fixed.
Calculate the total firefighting cost: the sum of time and money spent reacting to these symptoms per month. This number is usually shockingly high because each individual symptom feels small.
Do not try to fix any symptom yet. The goal of this step is to see the full picture of where your reactive time goes.

steps.description: For each symptom, trace the causal chain backward: what caused this symptom? And what caused that? Continue until you reach a cause you can actually change.

inputs.name: symptom-list
inputs.desc: All recurring symptoms with frequency and cost

outputs.name: causal-chains
outputs.desc: For each symptom, the chain of causes from symptom back to root cause (5 Whys or similar)

outputs.name: common-roots
outputs.desc: Root causes that appear in multiple causal chains (these are high-leverage intervention points)

process: For each symptom, ask 'why does this happen?' and record the answer. Then ask 'why does THAT happen?' and record. Continue 5 times or until you reach a cause you could prevent.

Be specific at each level. 'Because the process is bad' is not a cause. 'Because the handoff between team A and team B has no written specification, so each team interprets requirements differently' is a cause.

After mapping all chains, look for common roots: causes that appear in the causal chains of multiple symptoms. A root cause that drives 5 symptoms is a higher-leverage intervention point than one that drives 1.
Mark each cause in the chain as 'controllable' (you can change it) or 'uncontrollable' (external, cannot change). The intervention point must be the most upstream controllable cause.

steps.description: Score each potential intervention point by: number of symptoms it resolves, cost to fix, and how far upstream it is.

inputs.name: causal-chains
inputs.desc: All causal chains from symptoms to roots

inputs.name: common-roots
inputs.desc: Root causes shared across multiple chains

outputs.name: scored-interventions
outputs.desc: Each potential intervention point scored by: symptoms resolved (more = better), cost to fix (less = better), upstream distance (further = better)

outputs.name: top-intervention
outputs.desc: The single highest-leverage intervention point to address first

process: For each common root cause, count the number of downstream symptoms it drives. A root cause that eliminates 8 symptoms when fixed is more valuable than one that eliminates 2.

Estimate the cost to fix each root cause. Some root causes are cheap to fix (add a checklist, change a default setting, write a specification). Others are expensive (redesign a system, hire a person, change a vendor).
Score each intervention: (number of symptoms eliminated times monthly firefighting cost per symptom) divided by (cost to fix). The highest score is the best investment.
Select the top intervention. Do not try to fix multiple root causes simultaneously. Fix one, measure the impact, then move to the next.

steps.description: Implement the upstream fix and measure whether the downstream symptoms actually decrease.

outputs.name: fix-implementation
outputs.desc: The specific change made at the upstream intervention point

outputs.name: symptom-tracking-plan
outputs.desc: How to measure the frequency and cost of the downstream symptoms over the next 30-60 days

process: Design the specific change at the intervention point. If the root cause is 'no written specification for handoffs,' the fix is: write the specification, review it with both teams, and make it the required format for all handoffs.
Implement the change. Communicate what changed and why to everyone affected.
Set up tracking for all symptoms that this root cause was supposed to drive. Measure their frequency and cost for 30-60 days after the fix.
If the symptoms decrease as expected, the root cause analysis was correct. If not, either the fix was insufficient or the causal chain was wrong. Revisit the analysis.

steps.description: After the first upstream fix, re-audit the remaining symptoms and select the next highest-leverage intervention.

inputs.name: symptom-tracking-plan
inputs.desc: Tracking results showing which symptoms decreased

outputs.name: updated-symptom-list
outputs.desc: The remaining symptoms after the first fix, re-scored by frequency and cost

outputs.name: next-intervention
outputs.desc: The next highest-leverage upstream intervention point to address

process: Re-measure all symptoms. Some should have decreased. Others may be unchanged. A few may have increased (the fix may have shifted load).
Remove eliminated symptoms from the list. Recalculate the total firefighting cost with the remaining symptoms.
Re-run the leverage scoring on the remaining root causes. The rankings may have shifted because fixing one root cause sometimes weakens another root cause's impact.
Select the next intervention and repeat the cycle. Over time, each upstream fix reduces the total firefighting load, freeing capacity for proactive work instead of reactive work.

description: Audit and reduce decision fatigue by identifying every decision made in a day, classifying them by importance and reversibility, then eliminating or automating the low-importance ones to preserve cognitive resources for the decisions that matter.

steps.description: Log every decision you make for one full day, no matter how small.

inputs.name: typical-day-description
inputs.desc: What a typical workday looks like for you

inputs.name: known-decision-heavy-periods
inputs.desc: Times of day or week where you feel the most drained from decisions

outputs.name: decision-log
outputs.desc: Every decision made in one day, with timestamp and a brief description (expected: 30-70 decisions)

outputs.name: decision-count
outputs.desc: Total number of decisions logged

process: Carry a notebook or keep a note open on your phone. Every time you make a decision, no matter how small, record it with the time. Include: what to eat, what to wear, which email to answer first, how to respond to a message, which task to work on next, whether to attend a meeting.
Do not filter. The point is to capture everything. Small decisions are the ones that create fatigue because they are invisible but frequent.
At the end of the day, count the decisions. Most people are surprised: they make 50-100 decisions per day, and the cumulative cognitive cost is significant.
Note which decisions felt effortful (required thinking, comparison, or deliberation) versus automatic (you chose without thinking). The effortful ones are the fatigue drivers.

steps.description: Classify each decision on two axes: importance (high vs low impact on outcomes) and reversibility (easy to undo vs hard to undo).

inputs.name: decision-log
inputs.desc: All decisions from the logged day

outputs.name: classified-decisions
outputs.desc: Each decision placed in one of four quadrants: high-importance/irreversible (deliberate), high-importance/reversible (decide fast then adjust), low-importance/irreversible (standardize), low-importance/reversible (eliminate or automate)

outputs.name: quadrant-counts
outputs.desc: How many decisions fell in each quadrant

process: For each decision, rate importance: if you chose poorly, how much would it matter in a week? In a month? If the answer is 'not at all,' it is low importance.

For each decision, rate reversibility: if you chose poorly, how hard would it be to change course? Choosing what to eat for lunch is highly reversible. Choosing which vendor to sign a 2-year contract with is not.
Place each decision in the 2x2 matrix. Most decisions (typically 60-80%) are low-importance and reversible. These are the candidates for elimination.

The insight: you are spending cognitive energy on dozens of decisions that do not matter and could easily be changed even if you chose wrong. That energy should go to the few decisions in the high-importance quadrants.

steps.description: For each low-importance decision, design a rule, default, or automation that eliminates the need to decide.

outputs.name: elimination-rules
outputs.desc: Rules and defaults that remove the need to make low-importance decisions (e.g., 'always eat the same breakfast,' 'process email only at 10am and 3pm,' 'say no to all meetings without an agenda')

outputs.name: automation-list
outputs.desc: Low-importance decisions that can be automated through tools, templates, or delegation

process: For each low-importance/reversible decision, create a default rule. 'What should I wear?' becomes 'I wear the same 5 outfits on rotation.' 'Which email should I answer first?' becomes 'I answer in the order they arrived.'
For each low-importance/irreversible decision, create a standard. 'Which vendor for office supplies?' becomes 'Always use vendor X unless they are more than 15% more expensive.'
For recurring decisions, look for automation: can a tool, template, or delegation handle this? If you make the same decision every day, it should not require your brain.
Estimate how many decisions per day the rules and automation will eliminate. The target is to remove 50% or more of daily decisions.

steps.description: Protect cognitive energy for the high-importance decisions by scheduling them during peak mental hours and batching them.

outputs.name: decision-schedule
outputs.desc: When high-importance decisions will be made (ideally in the first 2-4 hours of the day, before fatigue accumulates)

outputs.name: decision-batching-plan
outputs.desc: Similar decisions grouped together so they are made in one session instead of scattered throughout the day

process: Identify your peak cognitive hours. For most people, this is the first 2-4 hours after waking (after any morning routine). Schedule high-importance decisions during this window.

Batch similar decisions together. All hiring decisions in one block. All budget decisions in one block. All strategic decisions in one block. Context-switching between decision types increases fatigue.
Never make high-importance/irreversible decisions at the end of a long day. If forced to, defer to the next morning.

Create a decision-making ritual for high-importance items: define the decision in writing, list the options, score each option against 2-3 criteria, choose, and record the rationale. The ritual prevents impulsive choices during low-energy moments.

steps.description: Monitor decision fatigue over time by tracking decision quality and energy levels throughout the day.

outputs.name: fatigue-tracking-results
outputs.desc: Daily energy and decision quality ratings over a 2-week period

outputs.name: system-adjustments
outputs.desc: Adjustments to the rules, schedule, and batching based on what is working and what is not

process: Rate your energy level at 3 points each day (morning, midday, evening) on a 1-10 scale for 2 weeks.
Note when you made decisions you later regretted. Were they during low-energy periods? Were they decisions that should have had a default rule?
After 2 weeks, review: did the elimination rules hold? Which rules did you follow consistently and which did you abandon? The abandoned rules may need redesign.

Adjust the system: add new rules for decisions you are still making unnecessarily, remove rules that create more friction than they save, and shift the schedule if your peak hours turned out to be different than expected.

description: Apply second-order thinking to any decision: map the immediate consequences, then the consequences of those consequences, then the consequences of those. Most people stop at first order and get surprised by second-order effects.

steps.description: State the decision clearly and list the realistic options (including doing nothing).

inputs.name: options
inputs.desc: The options you are considering (if known)

outputs.name: framed-decision
outputs.desc: The decision stated as a specific choice between specific options

outputs.name: option-list
outputs.desc: All options including the default (do nothing / status quo), each described in one sentence

process: State the decision as: 'I am choosing between [option A], [option B], and [option C].' If you cannot state it this way, the decision is not yet clear enough to analyze.
Always include the 'do nothing' option. Doing nothing is a choice with its own consequences. Ignoring it biases the analysis toward action.
Limit to 3-4 options. More than 4 creates analysis paralysis. If you have more, eliminate the weakest before proceeding.
For each option, write a one-sentence description of what it involves. This ensures everyone analyzing the decision has the same understanding of each option.

steps.description: For each option, list the immediate, direct consequences that will happen in the first days or weeks.

outputs.name: first-order-consequences
outputs.desc: For each option: 3-5 immediate consequences (things that will happen directly and quickly as a result of choosing this option)

outputs.name: first-order-confidence
outputs.desc: Confidence level for each consequence (high = very likely, medium = probable, low = possible)

process: For each option, ask: 'If I choose this, what happens immediately?' List 3-5 direct consequences.
First-order consequences are the ones most people already think about. They are obvious: 'If we raise the price, some customers will leave.' This is the easy part.
Rate your confidence in each consequence. High confidence means you have evidence or experience. Low confidence means you are guessing.
Note: first-order consequences are necessary but insufficient for good decisions. The interesting effects are at the second and third order.

steps.description: For each first-order consequence, ask 'and then what?' to map the second-order consequences.

outputs.name: second-order-consequences
outputs.desc: For each first-order consequence: 2-3 consequences of THAT consequence (what happens because the first-order effect happened)

outputs.name: second-order-surprises
outputs.desc: Second-order consequences that are counterintuitive or opposite to what the first-order effect would suggest

process: Take each first-order consequence and ask: 'And then what happens because of this?' If raising the price causes some customers to leave (first order), what happens next? The remaining customers may be higher-quality (second order). Competitors may interpret the price increase as confidence (second order).

Look specifically for second-order consequences that contradict the first-order effect. A price increase loses some customers (bad, first order) but increases perceived value for the remaining customers (good, second order).
This is where most analysis stops and where the best analysis begins. Second-order thinking reveals effects that are invisible from the first-order perspective.
Flag any second-order consequence that could become a feedback loop: a consequence that amplifies itself over time.

steps.description: Map third-order consequences for the most important second-order effects, and identify any feedback loops that could amplify or dampen over time.

outputs.name: third-order-effects
outputs.desc: For the most important second-order consequences: what happens after that? (Only map 2-3 third-order chains, not everything)

outputs.name: feedback-loops
outputs.desc: Any self-reinforcing or self-dampening loops identified across the three orders of consequences

process: Select the 2-3 most important second-order consequences and ask 'and then what?' one more time. Third-order consequences are speculative, so only invest the analysis in the most impactful chains.

Look for feedback loops: a third-order consequence that feeds back into a first-order cause. Example: higher prices lead to fewer but better customers (first/second), who generate better case studies (third), which attract more high-quality customers (feeds back to first). This is a positive feedback loop.
Also look for negative feedback loops: consequences that dampen themselves over time. These are self-correcting and less dangerous.

The feedback loops are the most important output of the entire analysis. A decision that triggers a positive feedback loop is much more valuable than one with only linear effects. A decision that triggers a negative feedback loop may undo itself.

steps.description: Synthesize the full consequence map across all three orders and choose the option with the best total trajectory, not just the best immediate effect.

outputs.name: option-trajectories
outputs.desc: For each option: the overall trajectory across all three orders (improving over time, degrading over time, or stable)

outputs.name: recommended-option
outputs.desc: The option with the best multi-order trajectory, with the rationale based on the analysis

process: For each option, assess the overall trajectory: does it get better over time (positive second and third-order effects outweigh negative first-order), or worse over time (positive first-order but negative downstream)?

The best option is often the one with the best trajectory, not the best first-order effect. An option with a slightly painful first-order effect but strong positive second and third-order effects is usually the right choice.
Conversely, avoid options with great first-order effects but degrading trajectories. These feel good now and create problems later.
Make the decision and record your analysis. The analysis is valuable not only for this decision but as a reference for future similar decisions.

description: Plan using constraints (anti-goals) instead of goals: define what you refuse to do, then operate freely within those boundaries. Constraint-based plans are more robust because they define the space of acceptable outcomes rather than one specific target.

steps.description: Define your anti-goals: the outcomes you refuse to accept, stated as hard boundaries.

inputs.name: planning-context
inputs.desc: What you are planning for (a project, a quarter, a year, a life phase)

inputs.name: past-regrets
inputs.desc: Previous outcomes that you wish you had avoided

outputs.name: anti-goals
outputs.desc: 5-10 outcomes you refuse to accept, stated as specific boundaries (e.g., 'I will not work more than 50 hours per week,' 'We will not take on more than 2 projects simultaneously')

outputs.name: anti-goal-rationale
outputs.desc: For each anti-goal, why this boundary exists (usually from a past experience where crossing it caused harm)

process: List every outcome from the past that you wish you had avoided. These are your anti-goals. 'I burned out last year working 70-hour weeks' becomes the anti-goal 'I will not work more than 50 hours per week.'
State each anti-goal as a specific, measurable boundary. 'I will not sacrifice my health' is too vague. 'I will not skip exercise more than once per week' is specific.

Include both outcome anti-goals (what you refuse to let happen) and process anti-goals (how you refuse to operate). Outcome: 'We will not ship with known critical bugs.' Process: 'We will not make strategic decisions in the last hour of the day.'
Limit to 5-10 anti-goals. Too many constraints leave no room to operate. The anti-goals should define the walls of the playing field, not every step on it.

steps.description: Check whether the constraints are feasible together: can you operate within all of them simultaneously?

inputs.name: planning-context
inputs.desc: The situation you are planning for

outputs.name: feasibility-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether all anti-goals can be satisfied simultaneously, or whether some conflict with each other

outputs.name: resolved-constraints
outputs.desc: The final set of anti-goals after resolving any conflicts (some may be relaxed to make the set feasible)

process: Check each pair of anti-goals for conflict. 'I will not work more than 40 hours per week' might conflict with 'I will launch the product by March 1' given the current scope.
If constraints conflict, decide which is more important. The more important constraint stays; the less important one is relaxed or removed.
Test feasibility by imagining a plan that satisfies all constraints. If you can envision at least one such plan, the constraint set is feasible.
If no feasible plan exists, you have learned something important: your expectations are internally contradictory, and something has to give. Better to discover this now than midway through execution.

steps.description: Map the space of acceptable actions: everything that does not violate any constraint is allowed.

outputs.name: action-space
outputs.desc: The set of strategies, tactics, and approaches that are available within the constraints

outputs.name: surprising-options
outputs.desc: Actions that are allowed by the constraints that you would not have considered under a traditional goal-based plan

process: Instead of asking 'what should I do?' ask 'what CAN I do within these boundaries?' The answer is usually a much larger space than a goal-based plan would suggest.
List the strategies and approaches that satisfy all constraints. Some will be obvious. Others will be surprising because traditional goal-based thinking would not have considered them.
The value of constraint-based planning is flexibility. Any path within the constraints leads to an acceptable outcome. This means you can adapt to changing circumstances without replanning.

Identify the options that are uniquely enabled by the constraint approach: paths that a goal-based plan would have excluded because they do not aim directly at the goal, but that avoid all the anti-goals.

steps.description: Execute within the constraints, adapting freely to circumstances as long as no constraint is violated.

outputs.name: execution-protocol
outputs.desc: The operating rules: pursue opportunity freely, check constraints before major decisions, raise an alarm if a constraint is at risk

outputs.name: constraint-monitoring
outputs.desc: How to monitor each constraint for early signs of violation

process: The execution rule is simple: do whatever seems best, but check each major decision against the constraint list before committing. If the decision would violate a constraint, do not do it. Otherwise, proceed.
Set up lightweight monitoring for each constraint. A weekly 5-minute check: am I still within all boundaries? If any constraint is within 20% of being violated, take corrective action.
This approach handles uncertainty well. You do not need to predict the future or follow a rigid plan. You need only avoid the anti-goals, and everything within the boundaries is acceptable.

When circumstances change (a new opportunity, a crisis, a market shift), do not replan. Ask: does this change violate any constraint? If not, adapt freely. If it does, which constraint is at risk and can we protect it?

steps.description: Review and evolve the constraint set periodically: some constraints become irrelevant, and new ones become necessary.

outputs.name: constraint-review
outputs.desc: Each constraint assessed: still relevant, needs tightening, needs loosening, or should be retired

outputs.name: new-constraints
outputs.desc: New anti-goals that have emerged from experience during the execution period

process: Review each constraint: was it ever at risk of being violated? If it was never even close, it might be too loose (could be tightened) or irrelevant (could be retired).
If a constraint was violated, what happened? Was the consequence as bad as expected? If worse, tighten the constraint. If milder, the constraint was correctly set.
Add new constraints from recent experience. If something happened during execution that you wish you had prevented, it becomes a new anti-goal.
The constraint set should evolve over time. As you learn what really matters and what does not, the boundaries become more precise and the operating space becomes better defined.

description: Run a structured after-action review (US Army AAR method): what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why the difference, and what will be done differently. More rigorous than 'lessons learned' because it forces comparison against a stated plan.

steps.description: Document what was supposed to happen (the plan) and what actually happened (the outcome), side by side.

inputs.name: event-description
inputs.desc: The project, event, campaign, or period being reviewed

inputs.name: original-plan
inputs.desc: The plan as it was stated before execution began

outputs.name: plan-column
outputs.desc: What was supposed to happen, broken into specific milestones and metrics

outputs.name: actual-column
outputs.desc: What actually happened, using the same milestones and metrics

outputs.name: delta-list
outputs.desc: Every point where the actual diverged from the plan, whether positive or negative

process: Retrieve the original plan. Use the actual documented plan, not a reconstructed memory of what the plan was. Memory rewrites the plan to match the outcome.
Break the plan into specific, measurable milestones. 'Launch on time' becomes 'Ship version 1.0 by March 15.'
For each milestone, record the actual outcome using the same metric. 'Shipped version 1.0 on April 2 (18 days late).'

List every delta, positive and negative. Include things that went better than planned (these are as instructive as failures) and things that were not in the plan at all (unplanned events that affected the outcome).

steps.description: For each significant delta, ask why. Trace the causal chain until you reach a cause that was within your control.

inputs.name: delta-list
inputs.desc: All deltas between plan and actual

outputs.name: root-causes
outputs.desc: For each major delta: the chain of causes from the delta to the root cause, including whether the root cause was controllable

outputs.name: controllable-causes
outputs.desc: Root causes that were within the team's control (these are the actionable findings)

process: Prioritize the deltas by impact. Not every delta needs a root cause analysis. Focus on the top 3-5 deltas (the largest positive and negative differences).

For each prioritized delta, ask 'why' repeatedly until you reach a cause that was within your control. 'We shipped late because testing took longer because we found more bugs because the code had more defects because the spec was ambiguous.' The controllable cause is 'the spec was ambiguous.'
Separate controllable from uncontrollable causes. An earthquake is uncontrollable. A missing specification is controllable. Focus the lessons on the controllable causes.
For positive deltas (things that went better than planned), trace the cause too. Understanding why something went right is as valuable as understanding why something went wrong.

steps.description: Extract specific, actionable lessons from the root causes.

outputs.name: lessons
outputs.desc: Specific lessons stated as: 'In situation [X], do [Y] instead of [Z], because [evidence from this event]'

outputs.name: lesson-owners
outputs.desc: Who is responsible for implementing each lesson

process: For each controllable root cause, write a lesson in the format: 'In situation [X], we should [Y] instead of [Z].' The lesson must be specific enough to act on.
'Write better specs' is not a lesson. 'Before starting development, walk the team through 3 edge cases per spec section and resolve ambiguities in writing' is a lesson.
Assign an owner to each lesson. A lesson without an owner is a nice thought that will never be implemented.
Limit to 3-5 lessons. More than 5 and none will be implemented. Choose the lessons with the highest impact on future outcomes.

steps.description: Integrate the lessons into the actual processes, checklists, and templates that the team uses. A lesson that lives only in a report will be forgotten.

outputs.name: process-changes
outputs.desc: Specific changes to existing processes, checklists, templates, or workflows that embed the lessons

outputs.name: verification-plan
outputs.desc: How to verify in the next project that the lessons were actually applied

process: For each lesson, identify the specific process, checklist, template, or workflow where it should be embedded. The lesson 'walk through 3 edge cases per spec section' becomes a checklist item on the spec template.
Make the change to the process document now, during the review. Do not create a separate action item to update the process later. If you leave the review without the change made, it will not happen.

Set up a verification trigger: at the start of the next similar project, check whether the process changes were followed. The trigger should be automatic (a checklist item, a meeting agenda point), not dependent on someone remembering.
Review the lessons from the previous AAR at the start of each new project to reinforce them. Lessons fade from memory within weeks if not actively reinforced.

description: Design the minimal viable process for any recurring task: start with zero process and add structure only when pain appears. Produces leaner processes that contain only the steps that have proven necessary.

steps.description: Document the current process exactly as it runs today (not how it is supposed to run) and measure how much of it is actually followed.

inputs.name: process-to-redesign
inputs.desc: The recurring task or workflow you want to streamline

outputs.name: actual-process
outputs.desc: The process as people actually execute it (observe, do not ask; people describe the ideal, not the real)

outputs.name: compliance-rate
outputs.desc: What percentage of the official process is actually followed (typically 40-60%)

process: Observe the process being executed 3-5 times. Watch what people actually do, not what they say they do. The gap between stated and actual process is where waste hides.
Document each step in the actual process, including workarounds, shortcuts, and skipped steps. These are not violations; they are signals that the skipped steps were unnecessary.

Calculate the compliance rate: what percentage of the official process steps are actually performed? Steps below 50% compliance are candidates for removal (if people skip them and outcomes are fine, the steps are waste).
Identify which steps, when skipped, cause problems. These are the essential steps. All other steps are candidates for removal.

steps.description: Strip the process to zero and define the absolute minimum: what is the fewest steps that produce an acceptable outcome?

outputs.name: essential-steps
outputs.desc: The 2-4 steps that are absolutely required for an acceptable outcome (if any of these are skipped, the outcome is unacceptable)

outputs.name: removed-steps
outputs.desc: Steps removed from the process, each with the reason (never followed, no impact when skipped, redundant with another step)

process: Start from zero: no steps. Ask: what is the first thing that absolutely must happen for an acceptable outcome? That is step 1.
Add steps one at a time, only if the outcome would be unacceptable without them. Stop adding when the outcome is acceptable. You will end up with 2-4 essential steps for most processes.
For each removed step, document why it was removed. This prevents someone from adding it back later without understanding the analysis.
The minimal process should feel uncomfortably lean. If it feels comfortable, you probably kept too many steps. Test it by running the minimal version 3-5 times before adding anything back.

steps.description: Run the minimal process and add steps back ONLY when specific pain appears (a defect, a failure, a rework cycle).

outputs.name: pain-log
outputs.desc: Record of problems that occurred during the minimal process trial, each with the date, impact, and whether adding a step would have prevented it

outputs.name: added-back-steps
outputs.desc: Steps added back to the process because specific pain proved they were necessary

process: Run the minimal process for 2-4 weeks. Track every problem that occurs.
For each problem, ask: would a process step have prevented this? If yes, add that specific step. If not (the problem was a one-time event or an external factor), do not add a step.
The key discipline: only add a step when pain proves it is needed, not when fear suggests it might be needed. Fear-driven process steps are the source of most process bloat.
Each added step must specify: what triggers it, who does it, what the output is, and what problem it prevents. A step without a clear purpose will be skipped.

steps.description: After the trial period, freeze the process: the minimal steps plus only the pain-driven additions become the new standard.

outputs.name: final-process
outputs.desc: The frozen process: minimal steps + pain-driven additions, documented simply

outputs.name: process-rationale
outputs.desc: For each step: why it is in the process (which specific problem it prevents)

process: Combine the essential steps with the pain-driven additions. This is your new process.
Document it simply: one page maximum, with each step described in one sentence. If the documentation is longer than one page, the process is too complex.
Include the rationale for each step: 'This step exists because during the trial, problem X occurred 3 times when this step was not performed.' The rationale prevents blind removal later.

Communicate the new process to everyone who uses it. Emphasize that any suggested additions must go through the pain-driven protocol: propose the step, wait for the pain to appear, then add it if the pain proves it necessary.

steps.description: Review the process every 6 months and remove any step that has not prevented a problem since the last review.

outputs.name: pruning-results
outputs.desc: Steps retained (with evidence of value in the past 6 months) and steps pruned (no evidence of value)

outputs.name: updated-process
outputs.desc: The process after pruning

process: For each step, ask: in the past 6 months, has this step prevented a problem? If no one can cite a specific instance, the step may no longer be necessary.
Remove steps that have not proven their value in 6 months. If the removal causes pain, add the step back through the pain-driven protocol.
Processes accumulate steps over time like barnacles. Without periodic pruning, the minimal viable process gradually becomes the bloated process you started with.
After pruning, re-document and re-communicate. The process should always be shorter after a review, never longer, unless new pain has appeared.
